## Introduction

### Learning goals

In this lecture, you will learn how to:

- Set up and use the Claude extension in VS Code Server at OSC
- Use Claude to ask questions about, write, and edit code
- Let Claude act as an "agent" that runs commands and works across files ---
  and keep that safe with permission settings and Git
- Give Claude standing instructions with a `CLAUDE.md` file

### Why Claude in VS Code Server?

- Recap from w8a: browser chat → in-IDE chat → agents
- Why this setup:
  - University-compliant usage, so the data privacy rules from w8a
    work in our favor here (TODO: exact wording once key provisioning is settled)
  - Runs inside our familiar VS Code Server, so on a **compute node** ---
    matters once the agent starts running commands
  - No extra local setup
- What it does _not_ do: inline "ghost text" suggestions as you type
  - Briefly explain what those are (1-2 screenshots from the bonus page)
  - Pointer to the [bonus page on GitHub Copilot](../bonus/copilot.qmd)
  - Teaching rationale, briefly: chat/agent output is something you
    review deliberately, while ghost text is easy to accept without reading

## Writing and editing a script

Reuse the FastQC sequence from 2025:

1. > Write a Bash script that runs FastQC for a single FASTQ file. The FASTQ file should be an argument to the script

   - Claude proposes creating a file → show the diff/approval view → accept
2. > Include strict bash settings in the script
   - Proposed edit shown as a diff → review → accept
   - Callback to `git diff` from week 5
3. > Now add an argument for the output directory
4. > Add code to print the current date before and after running FastQC

- Introduce **permission modes**: ask before every edit vs. accept edits
  automatically vs. plan mode (TODO: exact names in the extension).
  Recommendation for this course: keep "ask before edits" on.
- Compare the result to the scripts we wrote in week 7: what does it do
  differently from our conventions? (Sets up the `CLAUDE.md` section below.)

## Letting the agent run commands

- The agent can propose shell commands; you approve or deny each one
- Example:

  > Run this script on one of the FASTQ files in garrigos/fastq

  - Will it figure out how to make FastQC available (module/container, week 6)?
  - Show the approval prompt; discuss **what to never approve blindly**
    (`rm`, `mv`, anything writing outside your dir, `sbatch` loops, etc.)
- **Key point:** an agent that can run `trim_galore --help` can check
  its own claims. Revisit the TrimGalore hallucination from w8a:

  > How can I tell TrimGalore that my reads use Illumina two-color chemistry?

  - Did it guess, or did it check the help output? Does that change the answer?
  - (Connects to GA4 Part D)

## Agent tasks across files

- Plan first, then act: ask for a plan, review it, then let it proceed
- Examples from 2025 that worked well:

  > Write a similar script but to run the program TrimGalore

  - It should find your week 7 TrimGalore script(s) and build on them ---
    show that it looked around the project

  > Create a script to run the program featureCounts on BAM files in a given directory

  - Note: there are no BAM files yet; what does it assume about file names?
    (2025: Copilot invented `sample1_R1.fastq`-style names)

## Git as your safety net

- Before letting an agent edit files: `git status` clean, commit first
- After: `git diff` to review everything it changed, also files you didn't look at
- Undo with `git restore` (or discard specific hunks in the VS Code Source Control panel)
- Optionally: ask Claude to write a commit message, then edit it yourself

## Standing instructions with `CLAUDE.md`

- What it is: a Markdown file that Claude reads at the start of every session
- Create one (TODO: show `/init` vs. writing it by hand)
- Example content based on this course's conventions:

  ```markdown
  # Conventions for shell scripts in this project
  - Start scripts with `#!/bin/bash` and `set -euo pipefail`
  - Use uppercase variable names, copied from positional arguments
    with descriptive names
  - Report the date and program version at the start and end
  - Don't use `--cores` options unless asked
  ```

- Re-run one of the earlier prompts and compare the output
- (Same idea as Copilot's `.github/copilot-instructions.md`)

## Good habits and pitfalls with agents

- Review every edit and command; you own the result
- Agents may claim "this works" without having run it --- run it yourself
- Context: long conversations get worse; start fresh for a new task
  (TODO: `/clear` / new-conversation button in the extension)
- Tokens and cost: briefly what a token is
  ([link](https://posit-conf-2025.github.io/llm/slides/slides-02.html#/actually-tokens-not-words));
  agents use far more tokens than chat
- Never paste secrets (passwords, API keys) into prompts
- Shared project dir: the agent can see what _you_ can see
